newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia targets Aborigines in latest AIDS fight.
newsitem.headline: Australia targets Aborigines in latest AIDS fight.

text.p: Australia's fight against AIDS is to target Aborigines following fears of a potential epidemic among indigenous people, Health Minister Michael Wooldridge said on Wednesday.
Launching Australia's HIV/AIDS strategy for the next three years, Wooldridge said gay men and aboriginal people would be given the highest priority for the containment of the disease.

"The vast majority of HIV infections in Australia remain among homosexually active men, although there is the potential for an emerging epidemic among aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people," he said.

Australia has successfully reduced its rate of HIV infection in recent years, to about 480 new cases a year, but the rate of diagnosis among indigenous people is increasing, according to the national strategy report.
To date only about 100 cases of HIV have been found among indigenous people, offering encouragement to health workers.
"It hasn't substantially entered (aboriginal communities) so we do have a real opportunity," Wooldridge said.
The report said the rate of infection from heterosexual contact was three times as great among indigenous people than in the general population, suggesting more women were at risk.
Programmes would emphasise overall sexual health, aiming to counter the very high rates of sexually-transmitted diseases in many communities, which increase the potential to pass on HIV.
The change is part of a broadening of the national strategy to include other blood-borne diseases, such as hepatitis C and other sexually-transmitted diseases.
Wooldridge also raised concerns about the rapid growth of HIV infection in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly in neighbouring Papua New Guinea.
"We're kidding ourselves if we think we can be immune from what is happening among our neighbours," he said.
Papua New Guinea faced a real challenge to combat the disease, with an apparent "explosion" of HIV in the Fly and Daru regions in the southern part of the South Pacific country.
Its rapid spread had a direct effect on Australia with some 30,000 visits a year from PNG to the Torres Straits Islands off Australia's northern coast, he said.
The report said an estimated 4.7 million adults were infected in South and Southeast Asia by mid-1996.
Wooldridge said Australia was keen to work with regional governments to help combat AIDS, but had to operate within national structures.
In all some 15,600 Australians are estimated to have contracted HIV up until June 30, 1996. Of these 6,877 have progressed to AIDS and 4,962 have died.
However the rate of HIV infection has fallen dramatically from a high of 3,000 a year in the early 1980s to level out at about 500 a year.
